findings.title: Deserialization ignores serialized category keys
findings.desc: `deserializeCatalog` discards each entry’s `category` and derives the key from `entry.best` by replaying it through `recordPhoto`. A corrupted or mismatched payload can therefore silently load into a different catalog (or lose entries), rather than rejecting invalid persisted data; the redundant category should be validated against the derived category or omitted from the format.

findings.title: Deserialization accepts invalid capture counts
findings.desc: `deserializeSession` copies `data.captureCount` without validating that it is a finite, non-negative integer. Malformed save data can produce negative counts or cause `captureToSession` to yield `NaN`/string concatenation instead of a valid shutter count.

findings.title: Serialized category is silently ignored
findings.desc: `deserializeCatalog` never validates or uses `entry.category`; it reconstructs the category solely from `entry.best`. A corrupted or mismatched payload is silently rewritten under a different category, contrary to the serialized schema and making save corruption difficult to detect.

findings.title: Catalog payload shape is not validated
findings.desc: A version-1 JSON payload with missing/non-array `entries` or malformed entries will throw incidental runtime errors (or silently drop null-subject records) rather than being rejected as an invalid save. Since callers load parsed JSON via type assertions, corrupted save data can crash or produce a changed catalog.

findings.title: captureCount is accepted without validation
findings.desc: A parsed/corrupted save can supply a string, negative, fractional, or non-finite `captureCount`; a string causes later `captureToSession` calls to concatenate (for example `"0" + 1` becomes `"01"`), permanently corrupting session telemetry. Validate it as a non-negative safe integer during deserialization.

findings.title: Deserialization does not validate serialized structure
findings.desc: Beyond the version, arbitrary JSON is trusted as having an iterable `entries` array and valid photos; malformed saves can throw untyped runtime errors (such as when `entries` is absent) rather than a controlled persistence error. The same issue propagates through `deserializeSession` for malformed nested catalogs.

findings.title: UnsupportedVersionError constructor incorrectly logs NaN/undefined
findings.desc: If `foundVersion` is undefined or NaN, `JSON.stringify(foundVersion)` yields `"null"` (for undefined) or `"null"` (for NaN), which is misleading; better to stringify with `String(foundVersion)` for clarity.

findings.title: Floating-point equality check may fail
findings.desc: Using `===` to compare floating-point `total` scores after a serialization round-trip is fragile; should use an epsilon tolerance or round to a fixed precision.

findings.title: Redundant iteration in scoring
findings.desc: `sessionScore` iterates `discoveredEntries` to sum scores, but `categoriesDiscovered` and `completionFraction` also iterate internally; could be optimized by computing once if performance becomes critical.

findings.desc: Constant `COMPLETION_BONUS_WEIGHT` is used in `SessionScore` calculations but not exported, preventing external validation/display of weighting logic.

findings.title: String equality test for floating point numbers
findings.desc: `reloadedScore.total === score.total` uses strict equality on floating point numbers, which may fail due to IEEE 754 precision; should use an epsilon comparison.

findings.title: Score weight rationale not fully accounted for
findings.desc: Documentation states completion bonus should equal "one extra perfect (1.0) photo per category" for full catalog, but weight is `TOTAL_CATEGORIES` while max `collectionQuality` is `TOTAL_CATEGORIES * 1.0`, making bonus equal to quality not an extra quality-equivalent.

findings.title: Session reuses catalog's version constant
findings.desc: `serializeSession` tags the envelope with `CATALOG_FORMAT_VERSION` instead of a dedicated session format version, so a future change to the session envelope shape (independent of the catalog shape) would have no way to be versioned/detected without also bumping (and thus conflating) the catalog's version.

findings.title: Session version reuses catalog's version constant
findings.desc: `SerializedSession.version` is validated against `CATALOG_FORMAT_VERSION` with no independent `SESSION_FORMAT_VERSION`. This ties the session wire format to the catalog format, so a catalog-only schema change forces an unrelated session version bump (or vice versa), making future migrations harder to reason about despite the module comment claiming this coupling is intentional.

findings.title: No structural validation of deserialized payloads beyond version
findings.desc: `deserializeCatalog`/`deserializeSession` only check the `version` field; malformed/corrupted `entries`/`best`/`captureCount` values (e.g. from a hand-edited or corrupted save file) will propagate into `recordPhoto` and can throw unhandled/confusing errors rather than a typed, catchable error like `UnsupportedVersionError`.

findings.title: "bytes" label is actually character count
findings.desc: `saved.length` on a JS string counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes; the log message `${saved.length} bytes` is misleading if the serialized JSON ever contains non-ASCII/multi-byte characters (harmless today since content is ASCII, but the label is inaccurate).

findings.title: Session and Catalog share one version number
findings.desc: `serializeSession`/`deserializeSession` reuse `CATALOG_FORMAT_VERSION`/`assertSupportedVersion` for the session's own top-level version tag. If the `Session` shape changes independently of `Catalog` (e.g. a new session-only field), there is no way to bump the session's version without also bumping the catalog's, so an old session payload could be silently accepted as valid under the same version number.

findings.title: Save/load can change the exact session score
findings.desc: `sessionScore` sums floating-point scores in catalog `Map` insertion order, while serialization sorts entries by category and deserialization rebuilds the map in that new order. Because floating-point addition is order-dependent, a round-trip can produce a slightly different `total`, violating the documented identical-score guarantee and causing the CLI’s exact equality check to report `NO`.

findings.title: Deserialization silently ignores serialized category keys
findings.desc: Each serialized entry includes a `category`, but deserialization derives the category solely from `best` and never verifies they match. Corrupted or edited saves can therefore silently restore a different catalog than represented by the payload instead of being rejected.

findings.title: Loaded session fields are not validated
findings.desc: `deserializeSession` accepts `captureCount` unchanged and the nested deserializers likewise assume structurally valid entries/photos; malformed JSON can yield negative, fractional, non-numeric, or concatenating capture counts and invalid scores, or throw incidental `TypeError`s. Since this API is explicitly intended for `JSON.parse` save data, it should validate runtime shape and numeric invariants before constructing live state.
